## Shake Shack: Hospitality at Scale


October 16, 2026


In this episode of Exceptional Leaders, Danny Meyer, Founder and Executive Chairman of Union Square Hospitality Group, reflects on the journey from opening one restaurant to launching the global chain Shake Shack, and shares how companies can maintain their culture and core principles as they scale.


**DANNY MEYER**


I always felt—incorrectly—I felt that growing was going to be selling out. And I had to convince myself that you can also sell up; you don’t have to sell out. And if you can actually use your growth to advance your culture and get better and create more jobs and do better things for more neighborhoods, that’s not a bad thing.


**JOHN MOORE**


Union Square Hospitality Group is behind some of New York’s most acclaimed restaurants and bars, including Gramercy Tavern, The Modern, Eleven Madison Park, and Union Square Café. But the business goes well beyond restaurants, spanning events, consulting, and professional development. And of course, there’s Shake Shack: a casual concept that grew from a hot-dog cart in Madison Square Park into a global brand. Today, Shake Shack is a publicly traded company that operates more than 700 locations across 24 countries with annual sales approaching $1.5 billion in 2025. Behind that growth is a business philosophy that founder and chairman Danny Meyer calls Enlightened Hospitality: putting people and culture at the center of how you build and scale a company. As a New Yorker and as part of Morgan Stanley’s Global Capital Markets team, I’ve followed the evolution of Union Square Hospitality Group and Meyer’s journey as an entrepreneur and author for many years. So we sat down to talk about hospitality, culture, growth, his new book, and what it takes to build a business that can scale. And we did it right here at the restaurant where it all began.


**JOHN MOORE**


So good morning, Danny. Thank you very much for joining us here at Union Square Cafe for the Morgan Stanley Exceptional Leaders series.


**DANNY MEYER**


I'm honored to be here.


J **OHN**


How was that idea of hospitality born in your thinking, your growing up, and how you made it a part of Union Square Cafe?


**DANNY**


Growing up in Saint Louis in the 60s and 70s, I loved going to restaurants, but it wasn't so much because the food was great back then. It was much more because of how we were treated. I always loved cooking. I always loved eating. My dad was in the travel business, primarily in Europe. And meanwhile, I moved to New York. The food was really good here but the hospitality wasn't. And meanwhile, I started thinking about some of the experiences I had had when I was cooking in Rome and some of the time I had spent in France also going to bistros. And then about the same time, I’d traveled a few times to California, where you started to see this café and bar and grill movement happening, and what all those places had in common—trattorias, bistros, and the bar and grill of, you know, the Bay Area in California—was that the food was really good. It was a very simple. But what they also had in common was the people who worked there were genuinely happy to see you. And so, it just hit me: wait a minute, why can't I take what I grew up with in Saint Louis, match it with the experiences that at that point I had had with really good food in France, Italy, California, and do something fresh? Which, by the way, today, there are thousands of restaurants that occupy this kind of space. But it may be hard to believe, but there just weren't that many in 1985.


**JOHN**


And the magic I always thought—because I started as an analyst in 1985 with Morgan


Stanley, and, you know, with some of those first paychecks, going to Union Square Cafe was a big deal—but the people were friendly.


**DANNY**


A whole paycheck?


**JOHN**


Yeah, well, not quite.


**DANNY**


Our prices were pretty low back then.


**JOHN**


But the environment was different. It was friendly. It was neighborhood. I meet people to this day who talk about the Tuesday night group that gathered at Union Square Cafe, but the magic really was in the staff, the welcoming.


So there were 10 years between Union Square Cafe and this restaurant. That was a tough move for you.


**DANNY**
It was a very tough move to go from one to two. And it was a tough move because I had promised myself that I didn't want to end up bankrupt, as I had seen my dad go a couple times, and I always associated his bankruptcy with growing his business. For right or for wrong.


**JOHN**
Thank you. Always beautiful.


**DANNY**
This restaurant is now 32 years old.


**JOHN**
It's incredible.


**DANNY**
And there's something kind of magical where the older it gets, the better it looks. And I wish that were true of me.


**JOHN**
You're doing—you’re doing fine.


**JOHN**


Union Square Café in 1985; Gramercy Tavern in 1994; Eleven Madison Park and Tabla in 1998. Meyer was becoming an icon in a specific New York neighborhood, running from Union Square to Madison Square Park. And during all this time, Meyer was developing his principles of hospitality and how to scale it, setting the scene for his biggest expansion yet.


**JOHN**


You're at Eleven Madison, this gorgeous restaurant, Tabla, and you decide, for really philanthropic reasons, to get behind a campaign to improve Madison Square Park. What wasn't back then, or some in a decade and a half ago, what it looks like today. And as part of that renewal campaign, you offered to start a hot dog cart.


**DANNY**


We created something called the Campaign for the New Madison Square Park. We brought in the Public Art Fund of New York City—wonderful public-private partnership—and asked them to curate a piece of art. The Target Corporation decided to get behind this community project. So, Target actually sponsored bringing in this artist from Thailand, had this idea of having four taxicabs on stilts, and he wanted to have a working hot dog cart that he designed right underneath the taxicabs. They came to me, and they said, “We need someone to operate this guy's hot dog cart.” And I said, “Well, sure, we'll do it. Let's make Chicago-style hot dogs with eight toppings so we can see if hospitality actually works at a hot dog cart.” It was the same thing we were doing in our full-service restaurants. And the lines for this hot dog cart were like 100 people long every single day. And we did that for three consecutive years; even when they took down the piece of art, the community said, “Please bring back the hot dog carts.” We did it again in 2002, 2003. And that's when I said, “Wait a minute, let's turn this into a permanent kiosk.”


**DANNY**
I had gone to these burger shacks and frozen custard places growing up in St. Louis. And so, really all I wanted to do was to kind of honor what I had loved growing up. How do you get independence from the telephone at home? You get in your car and go meet friends in the parking lot of a burger place. So, this is simply taking that idea and saying alright, “New Yorkers don't necessarily have an automobile culture…”


**JOHN**
But we have parks.


**DANNY**


But we have parks. And why not use the park as a gathering place?


**JOHN**
Yep.


**DANNY**


I’d read this book by a friend named Billy Shore, called *The Cathedral Within* , about creating community wealth. And so, I wanted what I would call Shake Shack to be a community wealth project. And here's what it meant: it lives somewhere between capitalism and philanthropy. The model was that we would gift this building to the park so the park would become our landlord. And so, a percentage of every sale would go right back into the park to make the park more beautiful and safer. And lo and behold, all these years later, we got a big company out of it. That was never the goal to do that. In fact, we didn't open a second Shake Shack for five years.


**JOHN**


I want you to describe for us a little bit about how fine dining and all the skills of a fine dining enterprise informed a more casual dining.


**DANNY**


We don't have tablecloths, we don't have flowers, we don't have waiters or waitresses. We don't have art on the walls. But here's what they all have in common: what they all have in common is a real devotion to sourcing the best possible ingredients. When we first started working with Pat LaFrieda the butcher, who had a lot to do with the success and why people fell in love with the Shack Burger—it’s only because we had been using his beef, both at Union Square Cafe and at Tabla. But you're also getting a dedication and commitment to hospitality. You're getting a commitment that the way someone makes you feel while they're handing you your tray of food is at least as important as how great that food tastes. And it's something that I learned a long time ago in the fine dining business, which is that having great food is table stakes; that what really, really matters even more is: how did we make you feel while we were creating that experience? And the big challenge and the big opportunity for a business like Shake Shack is: how do you scale that feeling over many, many places in many, many different cities? One of the ways we've learned to do that is to make each Shake Shack feel like it's your Shake Shack. We have something called the 80-20 rule: 80% of the design, 80% of the menu is going to be the same everywhere, but 20% of the design and 20% of the menu should be customized to where we are. So, for example, I'll never forget when we opened in New Haven. We found reclaimed wood from the bleachers at the original Yale Bowl. They became the walls of the restaurant. And then we had a special hot dog. It's called the Handsome Dan, which is the nickname of the Yale mascot. And guess what? Sometimes that kind of innovation leads to something that you can use throughout the whole company.


Once we decided to grow, which was a really hard thing for me to do, because again, I just… I always felt that—incorrectly—I felt that growing was going to be selling out, and I had to really convince myself that you can also sell up. You don't have to sell out. And that if you can actually use your growth to advance your culture and get better and create more jobs and do better things for more neighborhoods, that's not a bad thing.


**JOHN**


Well, it goes back to the whole question about profitability and growth, and you sort of make a point in the book that it took time, but you convinced your management team: not mutually exclusive concepts and that the profitability would fuel the growth and the growth would fuel the profitability, as long as it was done with the right culture. And your expansion at Shake Shack was incredible. I mean leading up to the IPO, which we had the good fortune of


of leading with-


**DANNY**


We had the good fortune of hiring you to do that.


**JOHN**


It was great. And 73—63—stores, I think, at the time of the IPO or so in 2015?


**DANNY**


63 or 65, I forget.


**JOHN**


What did it feel like to go public?


**DANNY**


First of all, I have this tremendous—had, still have—a push-me, pull-you relationship with growth, because I want to stay pure to who we are. And I don't ever want the growth to either dilute our excellence or our hospitality and certainly not our culture. And it took me a long time to figure out that you can do it all.


**JOHN**


And you also had internal succession, as sort of natural growth. How did you manage that?


**DANNY**


The hardest choice for me was really a foolish ego choice, which is: what happens when you lose the three letters CEO by your name? And it's the greatest thing I ever did. But it was, it was not an easy Rubicon to cross? Now I don't focus on the operations nearly as much as I used to. I focus much, much more on three things. They all start with C: one is culinary, one is creative, and the third is the big C, which is culture.


**JOHN**


Twenty years after publishing his bestseller, *Setting the Table* , Meyer is back with a new book: *What Could Possibly Go Right?* In it, he looks back at the highs and lows of his journey, sharing candid stories about the challenges, setbacks, and successes that shaped Union Square Hospitality Group. At the heart of the book is an idea Meyer calls Practical Optimism: not ignoring what can go wrong but choosing to focus on what could go right. It’s also the story of how he took his philosophy of Enlightened Hospitality and built a culture that could grow far beyond a single restaurant.


\[BACKGROUND CONVERSATION WITH RESTAURANT STAFF\]


**JOHN**


One of the things that always struck me, and it's through both books, is how you managed and dealt with mistakes. Things go wrong in restaurants. You tell hilarious anecdotes about ways-


**DANNY**


Hilarious to you.


**JOHN**


I know at the time they were hard, but you have a very deliberate philosophy about how to address mistakes.


**DANNY**


What if you could actually end up in a better spot because of how you handled the mistake, than if the mistake had never happened in the first place? And so that's when we created the five “A”s of mistake making. That's also when we created a whole concept of writing a great next chapter, which is that when we make a mistake, can we write a great next chapter? You're going to say, “Well, I went to Union Square Cafe last night. Do you know what happened? The owner spilled a glass of champagne all over my lap,” which I've done. You're going to tell everyone that story. I need to make sure that when you tell that story—because you will—


**JOHN**


That there’s a next chapter.


**DANNY**


-that you say, “But you want to know how they handled it?” And so that's why we have the five “A”s of mistake making, which is: number one, be aware, because if you're not aware, you're nowhere; number two, acknowledge it; number three, apologize for it; number four, act on it, like fix it; and number five, apply additional generosity so that when John tells the whole world Danny Meyer spilled champagne all over his lap, “You won't believe how those guys handled it.” I think that mistakes are a lot like waves. There's just one after the next in the ocean, and you don't distinguish yourself as a surfer because you tame the ocean of its waves. You distinguish yourself because when there is a wave, you don't get knocked off your surfboard.


**JOHN**


I was fascinated in the recent book about how you talk about interviewing people and some of the questions you asked. And one question that's stuck in my mind was asking an interviewee: what's the best gift they ever gave?


**DANNY**


I also would ask people a question about how they've used their sense of humor to further either their work life or their personal life, because I always thought that was, that was an essential thing. I never really wanted to work with people who were—whose default was—defensiveness. I wanted to work with people who understood that life is about surfing the waves and sometimes having a good sense of humor is good for everybody else on the team. So that's the kind of questions I was asking back then. The game we were playing was hospitality—how we made other people feel—and that we had a recipe. It only had two ingredients. It was 49 parts performance—how well we did the thing we did—and it was 51 parts hospitality—how well we made people feel. And at the heart of hospitality is a spirit of generosity. It's believing that when you give a gift to someone else, it's actually going to come back and pay you. And so, I was hiring people who had the kind of emotional skills that, interestingly, lent themselves to being great at hospitality.


Shake Shack allows us to really double down on the whole theory of 49 and 51 percent. We've never asked anyone to please show us on their resume where they've had experience making milkshakes.


**JOHN**


What do you ask them?


**DANNY**


Who they are. So we're really focused on the 51% when we hire people through here, because unlike The Modern, which is a two-star Michelin restaurant where you need to have had a lot of culinary training before you're going to get the job, we can teach people pretty quickly how to make a milkshake here. A really good milkshake. And so what we're really hiring for here is the 51%.


**JOHN**


Talk about that essentiality—what you're trying to sort of be the legacy, the touchstone of the culture.


**DANNY**


Hospitality is not the end. It's a means for something much more important, which I call essentially. And when I create a restaurant with my team—and sometimes we've succeeded at this and other times we haven't, by the way—but the goal is to create an essential restaurant, a restaurant that actually, because of its very existence, made people's lives better. And if, God forbid, it went out of business, people would actually miss it. So, I'm focused on that word essentiality. And I think maybe if ever I write another book—I didn't just say that because I'm not, I'm not planning that at all—but I would want to write about how essentially then leads to legacy, because that's what people remember the most.


**JOHN**


So, thank you again, Danny. And congratulations on the publication of *What Could Possibly Go Right?* And thank you for spending time this morning with us.


**DANNY**


I've enjoyed it. Thank you, John.


**JOHN**


Thank you, Danny.

## Transcript


**Danny Meyer:** I have this tremendous... push me, pull you relationship with growth because I wanna stay pure to who we are, and I don't ever want the growth to dilute our excellence or our hospitality, and certainly not our culture.


**John Moore :** For more than four decades, Danny Meyer, Founder and Executive Chairman of Union Square Hospitality Group, has built his career by questioning assumptions about how restaurants are supposed to work.


Early on, that meant challenging the idea that serious food required a formal setting—that warmth, familiarity and a sense of home somehow made a restaurant less ambitious. Later, it meant challenging some of his own assumptions about growth, culture and what could actually be scaled.


At the center of all of it is something difficult to measure: how a place makes people feel.


In 1985, Meyer opened Union Square Cafe in New York City’s Union Square neighborhood, followed by Gramercy Tavern, Eleven Madison Park, Tabla, and eventually, Shake Shack—a business that would test whether the hospitality Meyer practiced personally could become something an organization could teach, repeat and grow.


This is Exceptional Leaders, an original series from Morgan Stanley. I’m John Moore, Chairman of Global Capital Markets at Morgan Stanley. I’ve known Danny for years. I lived nearby when Union Square Cafe opened and became a regular, so I had a front-row seat to those early days. I sat down with him there to talk about how an instinct became a philosophy, what broke when he first tried to scale it, what he learned about building a culture that no longer depends on the founder being in the room, and his new book.


**John Moore:** So good morning, Danny. Thank you so much for joining us.


**Danny Meyer:** I'm honored to be here.


**John Moore:** I wanna go back in time, 1985, 27-year-old St. Louis kid, just came out of college. How was hospitality born in your thinking, your growing up, and how you made it a part of Union Square Cafe?


**Danny Meyer:** Yeah, it's something growing up in St. Louis in the '60s, I loved going to restaurants, but it wasn't so much 'cause the food was great back then. It was much more because of how we were treated, and I always loved cooking. I always loved eating.


I moved to New York. The food was really good here, but the hospitality wasn't, and meanwhile, I started thinking about some of the experiences I had had when I was cooking in Rome and also going to bistros.


And then about this same time I had traveled a few times to California where you started to see this cafe and bar and grill movement happening. And what all those places had in common, trattorias, bistros, and the bar and grill of the Bay Area in California, was that the food was really good.


It was very simple. They weren't being showy about it. It was much more about what was left off the plate than all the flourishes of what was on the plate. But what they also had in common was the people who worked there were genuinely happy to see you.


And so it just hit me, wait a minute, why can't I take what I grew up with in St. Louis, match it with the experiences that at that point I had had with really good food in France, Italy, California, and do something fresh.


**John Moore :** The idea sounds familiar now, but in 1985, it wasn’t. At the time, ambitious cooking was often associated with a certain kind of dining room: formal, polished and removed from the familiarity of everyday life. Meyer wanted to prove that great food could be taken seriously without sacrificing warmth, ease or a sense of welcome.


Union Square Cafe was his attempt to have both. And it worked. The restaurant quickly became one of New York’s most celebrated dining rooms. Living just a few blocks away, I was there often in those early years, and what I remember most was how personal it felt. Danny was there every night—greeting guests, watching the room and hand-picking the people around him. He could transmit his idea of hospitality himself.


The bigger test came when he tried to build restaurant number two. For years, Meyer resisted opening a second restaurant. Part of that hesitation was personal. He had watched his father go through two business bankruptcies, and growth became tied, in his mind, to the risk of losing what he had built. It took time for Meyer to separate expansion from failure. Nearly a decade after opening Union Square Cafe, he finally opened Gramercy Tavern—just a five-minute walk away.


**John Moore:** I know from being in the neighborhood for 25, 30 years, that growth was something that you were very intentional and deliberate about. Ten years between Union Square Cafe and, and Gramercy Tavern: how did you think about each of those locations, both in terms of locality, delegation, and then I wanna get back to your sort of overarching management style because you're going through a transition at this point, 'cause you can't be in five places in one night.


**Danny Meyer:** No. And I will say that going from Union Square Cafe to Gramercy Tavern was about the hardest, going from one to two, 'cause you have to understand, I was, I was the guy on the front door- Right ... greeting everybody- Yep ... for all those years.


I couldn't keep up with hiring at Gramercy Tavern as I had at Union Square Cafe. Then, opening Eleven Madison Park and Tabla four years after Gramercy Tavern opened, and opening those two restaurants four weeks apart from each other, that became the hardest thing I ever did.


And in fact, I think I managed it poorly.


The worst thing anyone could say to me in those years, not that they did anything wrong, it just, it stung, was when people would say, "You know what? The culture just doesn't feel the same anymore." Because that's when I really felt like I was failing. I felt like I was failing our team. I didn't bother asking a really important question though, which is, what do you mean when you say culture?


When you say the culture's changing, are you saying you don't see me as often as you once did? You're right, you don't. Are you saying that the boss you work for doesn't bring the same culture of hospitality to the staff? Which we call enlightened hospitality, which is we actually- Right ... prioritize the way our team takes care of each other, even over how well they take care of our guests, 'cause we think that one naturally leads to doing a great job with the next.


I didn't do a good job of asking them, "What do you mean when you say the culture doesn't feel the same?" 'Cause I knew the word, but we didn't have a common understanding of what that word meant.


**John Moore :** We leave Union Square Cafe and make the five-minute walk to Gramercy Tavern—the same trip Meyer made hundreds of times during dinner service, carrying with him the questions about growth and culture he was still trying to work out.


**John Moore :** Here we are, number two. What was the vision that you had for Gramercy Tavern, and how was it gonna be different from Union Square Cafe?


**Danny Meyer :** At that time, my favorite restaurant was Taillevent in Paris. Taillevent had three stars from Michelin longer than any other restaurant. They were really nice. They weren't the kind of restaurant where you felt like, "I have to be polite to them to make them be nice to me." They had a twinkle in their eye.


And I just asked myself, “What if Union Square Cafe had a baby with Taillevent?” We did everything we could to make it feel as if it had been here forever… it doesn't really matter as long as there's a real reason behind what we do, somehow it comes out.


**John Moore :** Gramercy Tavern would go on to become one of New York’s most acclaimed restaurants, earning nine James Beard Awards and a Michelin star. Gramercy Tavern taught Meyer that his restaurants could look different, feel different and still carry the same underlying values. But solving one problem exposed another. He had proven Union Square Cafe wasn’t a one-hit wonder. Now he had to define what made the culture work well enough for other people to recognize it, teach it and repeat it.


**Danny Meyer:** The game we were playing was hospitality, how we made other people feel, and we had a recipe. It only had two ingredients. It was 49 parts performance and it was 51 parts hospitality, and at the heart of hospitality is a spirit of generosity. It's believing that when you give a gift to someone else, it's actually gonna come back and pay you.


**John Moore:** Meyer began turning those ideas into a more deliberate system. Employees came first, followed by guests, the community, suppliers and investors—the idea being that each group strengthens the next. That shared framework gave a growing organization a common way to think about hospitality, even when Meyer himself wasn’t in the room.


Four years after Gramercy Tavern, Meyer opened Eleven Madison Park and Tabla just weeks apart—both becoming acclaimed New York restaurants in their own right.


From Gramercy Tavern, we continue north toward Madison Square Park, a small public greenspace across the street from the notable Flatiron Building. Meyer’s next experiment would come almost by accident. As Meyer became involved in restoring Madison Square Park, a neighborhood project gave him the chance to see if his approach to hospitality could work in an entirely different setting.


**John Moore:** You're at Eleven Madison, this gorgeous restaurant, and you decide for really philanthropic reasons to get behind a campaign to improve Madison Square Park, and as part of that neighborhood renewal campaign, you offer to start a hot dog cart. And, it kind of grew incredibly. Tell me the original intention-idea behind that hot dog cart.


**Danny Meyer:** Our landlord back then was MetLife. They owned the building and, so I said to them, even before signing the lease, "This sounds good. Before we even talk about the financial aspects of this lease, I wanna know that if I sign, you will join me in helping to renew Madison Square Park." And so we created something called the Campaign for the New Madison Square Park. We brought in the Public Art Fund of New York City, wonderful public-private partnership, and asked them to curate a piece of art.


The artist from Thailand, this was in 2001, right before 9/11, had this idea of having four taxi cabs on stilts, and he wanted to have a working hot dog cart that he designed right underneath the taxi cabs. And they came to me and they said, "We need someone to operate this guy's hot dog cart." And I said, "Well, sure, we'll do it." Let's make Chicago-style hot dogs because they've got eight classic toppings, so we can see if hospitality actually works at a hot dog cart. It was the same thing we were doing in our full-service restaurants, and the lines for this hot dog cart were like 100 people long every single day.


And we did that for three consecutive years. Even when they took down the piece of art the community said, "Please bring back the hot dog cart." So we did it again in 2002, 2003, and that's when I said, "Wait a minute. Let's turn this into a permanent kiosk." And so I wanted what I would call Shake Shack to be a community wealth project, and here's what it meant. It lives somewhere between capitalism and philanthropy.


The model was that we would gift this building to the park so the park would become our landlord, and so a percentage of every sale would go right back into the park to make the park more beautiful and safer. And lo and behold, all these years later, we got a big company out of it. That was never the goal to do that.


**John Moore:** What began as a neighborhood project became a much bigger test of Meyer’s ideas. Shake Shack removed many of the things he had traditionally used to create a restaurant experience: no tablecloths, no formal dining room, no traditional waitstaff. Could the feeling he had spent years cultivating in full-service restaurants survive when almost everything else around it changed?


**John Moore:** Describe for us how fine dining and all the skills of a fine dining enterprise informed a more casual dining enterprise, because those seem like very, very different worlds.


**Danny Meyer:** 100%. So when I think about a full service restaurant that happens to have tablecloths and silver, I don't really think about it dramatically different than how I was thinking about the hotdog cart or Shake Shack.


What they all have in common is a real devotion to sourcing the best possible ingredients. So if you go to Shake Shack, you're getting all natural beef, just like we would use at any of our restaurants. You're getting the finest chocolate in your chocolate milkshake, which you should have. ****


**Danny Meyer:** 63 or 65, I forget.

**John Moore:** Yeah ...


**Danny Meyer:** … to do. Again. 'Cause again, Incorrectly, I felt that growing was gonna be selling out, and I had to really convince myself that you can also sell up. You don't have to sell out.


**John Moore:** Yeah.


**Danny Meyer:** And that if you can actually use your growth to advance your culture and get better and create more jobs and do better things for more neighborhoods, that's not a bad thing.

**John Moore:** As the organization grew, Meyer also had to change the way he led it. He began putting many of those lessons into writing. His 2006 book, Setting the Table, gave his philosophy of hospitality a language and a way to share it beyond his own restaurants.


Nearly two decades later, What Could Possibly Go Right?: The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture returned to those ideas from a different vantage point—after years of growth, mistakes and course corrections.


**John Moore:** Tell us about the distinction, you write about it, between microcaring and micromanaging.


**Danny Meyer:** Yeah. So, just like in a car, you don't only drive in one gear. If you've ever driven a stick shift and even if you've driven an automatic, your car knows- Yeah ... exactly what gear it should be, and it changes as the driving conditions change. But so too do we need to have different gears when we're leading people. Sometimes it's, I know what I want. Sometimes it's trust and delegate. Sometimes it's, let's make a democratic decision and you need to have different gears, and sometimes I didn't understand that.


And one of the things I wrote about in What Could Possibly Go Right, the book almost feels like a compendium of Danny's biggest hits, the hits being mistakes. But underneath all of those mistakes has been a constant mindset that I've had that this could turn into something good, and that's why I called the book What Could Possibly Go Right. I think that mistakes are a lot like waves. There's just one after the next in the ocean. And you don't distinguish yourself as a surfer because you tame the ocean of its waves. You distinguish yourself because when there is a wave, you don't get knocked off your surfboard.


**John Moore:** For Meyer, leadership became less about avoiding the inevitable mistakes that come with growth and more about building an organization capable of learning from them. Which leads to the idea he now sees as the ultimate measure of whether a business has succeeded.


**Danny Meyer:** Over the years, I came to learn that the much bigger thing is hospitality, the way we made people feel, that would bring people back. And then I went a step further, and I realized that hospitality is not the end. It's a means for something much more important, which I call essentiality. The goal is to create an essential restaurant. A restaurant that actually, because of its very existence, made people's lives better. **John Moore:** From Union Square Cafe to Shake Shack, Meyer kept challenging assumptions—about what a restaurant should mean to its neighborhood, the cost of growth, and how a company’s values survive change.


As Union Square Hospitality Group grew and his role shifted, one question stayed constant: how do you build a business around how people feel—and can that feeling scale?

You just added the TSA wait times to the app. I didn't know that was possible.


**SCOTT**


We've also added technology on the app that if you opt in, we’ll track you, so we can know to wait for you for connecting gates. We want to do things like deliver food to your gate, if you need a connecting flight and you want to be able to order food. But one of the other things is, it'll give real time waits, trying to get really real-time data to customers, and we're the only airline that’s doing it.


**RAVI**


Moving to the topic of AI. So how does AI improve how United operates? And what does that mean for your passengers?


**SCOTT**


It's a great tool. It's going to do a lot of things—it does do a lot of things—really well. But I do not think that the primary use case of AI is replacing the work that everyone does. And if that's the primary use case, like, it's for sure a bubble, because we're spending way too much for that. Too many people are getting dependent on AI, and like thing that people are using AI for is summarizing documents. Like, that seems to me to be the number one use case. I actually want to read the book. Because all the cool learnings are, you know, on page 312 in a little paragraph that there's some cool insight, and I think you're going to miss all that.


The cool thing about AI is the things that you can do that were impossible or impractical before. One of my favorite examples is, anytime there's a delay or cancellation, I want the team to pretend I'm on the airplane and I've called the network operating center: “Why is my flight delayed?” Whatever they would tell me, I want to tell customers 100% of the time. We're better at it than any other airline in the world, but we're not even into the game yet. We're still in the pre-game. \[It’s\] really hard to do without AI. It's also going to help us, I think, in our network operating center, when we’re deciding which flights—when stuff happens, you know, when weather hits and airports close, like it's one of those problems that has multiple tentacles that can last for days: crew and maintenance and all kinds of other implications. And they're all stochastic, like you know, you don't know for sure what's going to happen down the line.


**RAVI**


Scott, you mentioned that Covid was an instance where the data pointed one direction, but your instinct took another direction. What is that moment today?


**SCOTT**


Oh, oil prices and the war in Iran. From the time that MEU left Asia for the Middle East, I thought the forward curve was wrong. I thought oil was going to be higher for longer. And so we’ve been preparing for that at United. The experts that I talked to back then all told me: worst case, the Straits of Hormuz are open by the end of March. I think oil prices are going to be higher for longer. We at United are preparing for that. That's our base case planning assumption. I think there may be an opportunity to take advantage of it when our competitors are managing more by hope instead of reality.


**RAVI**


Scott, so when you eventually do step out of the CEO role, what do you hope people would say that you changed about United and the industry?


**SCOTT**


I want to have United to have launched a new era in aviation—what it means to be an airline. A lot of it's going to be technology—the technology that takes all of the uncertainty and stress of travel. Make travel fun. And my second one is to leave behind a CEO who's better than me.


**RAVI**


Well, we won’t be making that change anytime soon. Scott, thank you for joining us. It has been real fun.


**SCOTT**


Thank you.


**RAVI**


Appreciate it.
